{{Short description|American economist}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=December 2025}}
'''Barry T. Hirsch''' (born 1949) is an [[Americans|American]] [[economist]] and the W.J. Usery Chair of the American Workplace at the [[Andrew Young School of Policy Studies]] of [[Georgia State University]].<ref>[http://www2.gsu.edu/~ecobth/ Profile of Barry T. Hirsch on the website of Georgia State University. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> Hirsch is one of the leading economists on the subject of [[industrial relations]] in the United States.<ref>[https://ideas.repec.org/top/top.lma.html Hirsch ranks among the top 3% of labour market researchers registered on IDEAS/RePEc. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref>

== Biography==

After earning a [[Bachelor of Arts|B.A.]] and a [[Ph.D.]] in economics from the [[University of Virginia]] in 1972 and 1977, respectively, Barry Hirsch took up a position as [[assistant professor]] at the [[University of North Carolina at Greensboro]]. There, he was first promoted to [[associate professor]] and full professor in 1979 and 1983, before moving on to [[Florida State University]] (FSU) in 1990. Shortly after becoming Distinguished Research Professor at FSU, Hirsch changed to the position of E.M. Stevens Distinguished Professor at [[Trinity University (Texas)|Trinity University]] ([[San Antonio, Texas]]), which he held until 2008. Finally, in 2008, Hirsch moved back to the East Coast by taking up the W.J. Usery Chair of the American Workplace at the [[Andrew Young School of Policy Studies]] of [[Georgia State University]], which he has held ever since. Beyond his academic positions, Hirsch maintains affiliations with the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation]], the [[IZA Institute of Labor Economics]],<ref>[https://www.iza.org/person/1312/barry-hirsch Profile of Barry Hirsch at IZA. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> and the [[Labor and Employment Relations Association]]. In terms of professional service, he performs editorial duties for the ''[[Journal of Labor Research]]'',<ref>[https://www.springer.com/social+sciences/journal/12122?detailsPage=editorialBoard Editorial board of the 'Journal of Labor Research'. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> ''[[Industrial Relations (journal)|Industrial Relations]]'',<ref>[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/1468232x/homepage/editorialboard.html Editorial Board of 'Industrial Relations'. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> ''[[Southern Economic Journal]]'',<ref>[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/23258012/homepage/editorialboard.html Editorial board of the 'Southern Economic Journal'. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> ''[[Industrial and Labor Relations Review]]'',<ref>[https://us.sagepub.com/en-us/nam/journal/ilr-review#editorial-board Editorial board of ILRR. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> and the ''[[Atlantic Economic Journal]]''.<ref>[https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/page/journal/23258012/homepage/editorialboard.html Editorial board of the Atlantic Economic Journal. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref>

== Research==

Barry Hirsch's research revolves primarily around [[labour economics]], especially [[industrial relations]], labour legislation and unions in the [[United States]]. In terms of research output, he ranks among the top 3% of economists registered on [[IDEAS/RePEc]].<ref>[https://ideas.repec.org/top/top.person.all.html#phi17 Barry Hirsch ranks 1568th out 56171 registered authors on IDEAS/RePEc. Retrieved June 30th, 2019.]</ref> Key findings of his research include:
* How do unions affect firm profitability and economic performance? Together with Robert A. Connolly and Mark Hirschey, Hirsch finds that reduces firm profitability by sharing the returns to firm-specific intangible capital, and thus disincentives R&D investment.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/1924515 | jstor=1924515 | title=Union Rent Seeking, Intangible Capital, and Market Value of the Firm | last1=Connolly | first1=Robert A. | last2=Hirsch | first2=Barry T. | last3=Hirschey | first3=Mark | journal=The Review of Economics and Statistics | date=1986 | volume=68 | issue=4 | pages=567–577 | doi=10.2307/1924515 | url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |url=https://research.upjohn.org/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1091&context=up_press |doi=10.17848/9780585283005 |title=Labor Unions and the Economic Performance of Firms |date=1991 |last1=Hirsch |first1=Barry T. |isbn=978-0-585-28300-5 }}</ref> Specifically, Hirsch finds unionized U.S. firms in the 1970s to have, on average, 10-15% lower market value and earnings than non-unionized equivalents, which might contribute to the declining U.S. unionization in the 1980s.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/2109688 | jstor=2109688 | title=Union Coverage and Profitability Among U.S. Firms | last1=Hirsch | first1=Barry T. | journal=The Review of Economics and Statistics | date=1991 | volume=73 | issue=1 | pages=69–77 | doi=10.2307/2109688 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> Overall, reviewing the evidence on union effects in the U.S. during the 1980s and 1990s, Hirsch concludes that unions effects have negatively affected the growth of U.S. firms, though without increasing their likelihood of business failure, and traces the breakdown of unions' role as workers collective voice in the U.S.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007%2Fs12122-004-1023-8.pdf | doi=10.1007/s12122-004-1023-8 | title=What do unions do for economic performance? | date=2004 | last1=Hirsch | first1=Barry T. | journal=Journal of Labor Research | volume=25 | issue=3 | pages=415–455 }}</ref>
* Another strand of Hirsch's research concerns wage differentials. For instance, Hirsch and Macpherson find that U.S. wage levels in predominantly female occupations were substantially lower throughout 1973-93, though they argue that only a third of the gender composition effect of occupations cannot be accounted for by occupational characteristics and unmeasured worker skill or taste differences.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/298381?mobileUi=0 | doi=10.1086/298381 | title=Wages and Gender Composition: Why do Women's Jobs Pay Less? | date=1995 | last1=MacPherson | first1=David A. | last2=Hirsch | first2=Barry T. | journal=Journal of Labor Economics | volume=13 | issue=3 | pages=426–471 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> With regard to part-time workers, Hirsch has argued that the gap in hourly wages between part-time and full-time workers is mostly due to differences between workers, especially in terms of skills that are built up more slowly for part-time workers.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/30038605 | jstor=30038605 | title=Why do Part-Time Workers Earn Less? The Role of Worker and Job Skills | last1=Hirsch | first1=Barry T. | journal=Industrial and Labor Relations Review | date=2005 | volume=58 | issue=4 | pages=525–551 | doi=10.1177/001979390505800401 | hdl=10419/20525 | hdl-access=free }}</ref> Finally, with regard to the union wage gap, in work with Edward Schumacher, Hirsch has highlighted that the gap between the wages of union and non-union workers in 1973-2001 was likely higher than estimated.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.1086/383112 | jstor=10.1086/383112 | doi=10.1086/383112 | title=Match Bias in Wage Gap Estimates Due to Earnings Imputation | date=2004 | last1=Hirsch | first1=Barry T. | last2=Schumacher | first2=Edward J. | journal=Journal of Labor Economics | volume=22 | issue=3 | pages=689–722 | hdl=10419/21456 | hdl-access=free }}</ref>
* Older workers in the U.S. faced particularly high barriers in the 1980s and 1990s in occupations with steep wage profiles, pension benefits and widespread computer use, with union coverage being a further cause of limitation for older and most older women concentrating in flex-time or part-time occupations.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/001979390005300303 | doi=10.1177/001979390005300303 | title=Occupational Age Structure and Access for Older Workers | date=2000 | last1=Hirsch | first1=Barry T. | last2=MacPherson | first2=David A. | last3=Hardy | first3=Melissa A. | journal=ILR Review | volume=53 | issue=3 | pages=401–418 | url-access=subscription }}</ref>
* Most recently, work by Hirsch, Kaufman and Zelenska has drawn attention to the various channels through which employment adjusts to [[minimum wage]]s, including through changes in prices, profits, wages, turnover and performance.<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/irel.12091 | doi=10.1111/irel.12091 | title=Minimum Wage Channels of Adjustment | date=2015 | last1=Hirsch | first1=Barry T. | last2=Kaufman | first2=Bruce E. | last3=Zelenska | first3=Tetyana | journal=Industrial Relations: A Journal of Economy and Society | volume=54 | issue=2 | pages=199–239 }}</ref>
